item.title: California bill recognizing 2 Islamic holidays nears Newsom’s desk
item.description: Gavin Newsom could soon decide whether California public schools and state workers get formal recognition of Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha holidays.
item.content:encoded:
California could soon formally recognize two of Islam’s most important holy days under legislation that would give state workers greater flexibility to take them off and allow public schools to close in observance of the holidays.

The measure, which overwhelmingly passed the state Assembly and is awaiting Senate action, would recognize Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha in state law and could soon head to Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom’s desk.

Assembly Bill 2017, introduced by Democratic San Francisco Assemblymember Matt Haney, passed the Assembly 64-1 in late May. It must clear the Senate before the legislative session ends Monday to reach Newsom.

TRUMP DOJ EXPANDS RELIGIOUS LIBERTY PROTECTIONS AFTER MAJOR SUPREME COURT RULINGS

The bill would let state employees use existing paid holiday credits to take time off for Eid. Public schools and community colleges could also close for the holidays.

"California is home to one of the largest and most vibrant Muslim communities in the country, and their traditions deserve recognition and respect," Haney said in a news release about the bill in March. "No student should have to choose between celebrating one of the holiest days of their faith and showing up to school, and no worker should feel they have to sacrifice their religious observance."

Haney also said the bill is also about treating Muslim Californians equally.

"AB 2017 is about making sure Muslim Californians are seen, valued, and treated with the same dignity as every other community in our state," he said.

Eid al-Fitr, or the "Festival of Breaking the Fast," marks the end of Ramadan, the Islamic holy month when Muslims fast from dawn to sunset. Eid al-Adha, or the "Festival of Sacrifice," commemorates the willingness of the Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) to sacrifice his son in obedience to God.

CALIFORNIA SCHOOL DISTRICT SUED OVER FIELD TRIP TO MOSQUE WHERE STUDENTS ALLEGEDLY DONNED MUSLIM GARB

Supporters say the bill would make it easier for Muslim workers and students to take part in Eid prayers and spend the holidays with their families.

"For decades, Muslim families across the state have had to navigate an unfair balancing act between their faith and their academic or professional obligations," Oussama Mokeddem, legislative and government affairs director for the Council on American-Islamic Relations’ (CAIR) California chapter, said in a statement in July. "AB 2017 is a meaningful step toward ensuring Muslim students can celebrate Eid with the same dignity, respect, and accommodation afforded to other faith communities."

Hala Hijazi, founder of the Muslim Impact Council, recalled missing Eid with her family earlier in her career while working for the city of San Francisco.

"It was really painful to not be with my family," Hijazi told the Sacramento Bee. She said her family would go to lunch after Eid al-Fitr services and give gifts to the children.

The California Family Council, a conservative Christian advocacy group, opposes the bill’s school provisions, while saying it supports allowing students to take time off for religious holidays.

FEDERAL COURT UPHOLDS TEXAS LAW REQUIRING TEN COMMANDMENTS IN PUBLIC CLASSROOMS

The group objects to language allowing schools to hold exercises "acknowledging and celebrating the meaning and importance" of Eid. It also criticized a provision allowing the State Board of Education to develop a model curriculum guide for those exercises.

"No California statute authorizes public schools to hold exercises celebrating the meaning of Christmas, Easter, or Good Friday," the group said in a May statement, arguing Christian and Jewish holidays have not received comparable treatment. "The asymmetry is written into the law."

If signed into law, Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha would join other holidays California has recognized, including Lunar New Year and Diwali.

California would not be the first state to recognize the Eid holidays. Washington was the first, according to the Sacramento Bee. Hijazi told the newspaper that California’s proposal would go further by allowing state workers to use paid holiday credits, while Washington allows unpaid time off.

item.title: What Meta's new teen restrictions mean for young people
item.description: Meta's new teen accounts settlement sets a default two-hour daily limit on Instagram and Facebook, plus night mode and school mode restrictions.
item.content:encoded:
If you have ever asked a teenager to put down a phone and heard, "Just one more minute," you already know how hard screen limits can be to enforce.

Now Meta has agreed to a sweeping child-safety settlement that could reshape how teens use Facebook and Instagram across much of the United States.

A judge approved the agreement on Aug. 27. Under the deal, Meta will put a default two-hour daily cap on teen use of Facebook and Instagram combined. It will also restrict most app access overnight. Meanwhile, parents will get stronger control over settings teens may want to change.

The agreement goes well beyond a screen time reminder. Here's what will change, how the limits work, what Meta told CyberGuy and what parents can do now.

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats , has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.

Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com

TOO MUCH SCREEN TIME MAY TRIGGER LASTING BRAIN DELAYS, TOP HEALTH OFFICIAL WARNS

With the judge's approval, the agreement is now in effect, but the new protections will roll out over the coming months. Most of the major requirements have a six-month compliance deadline, while some features are due sooner. Here's how the biggest changes break down for teens and parents.

Meta will apply a default two-hour daily limit across Facebook and Instagram combined. Time spent scrolling on either app counts toward the total. In addition, Meta says it will count usage across multiple accounts when it detects that one teen operates more than one account.

Direct messaging, time spent in settings and qualifying long-form audio or video are excluded from the two-hour limit. Under the agreement, qualifying long-form content generally means audio or video that lasts at least 22 minutes and has not been artificially extended.

A teen can only turn off the two-hour limit with a parent's permission. That creates a much firmer stopping point than another reminder that can be dismissed.

Night Mode will block most Facebook and Instagram activity from midnight to 6 a.m. During that window, teens will no longer be able to view or post to areas such as Feed, Stories, Explore or Reels.

Direct messaging will remain available. That exception lets teens continue communicating with friends and family. For families dealing with late-night scrolling, this could create a clearer boundary without requiring someone to change the setting every evening.

Meta will also disable push notifications by default from 10 p.m. to 7 a.m., except for urgent account security or platform integrity alerts. Parents using supervision can change that setting.

School Mode focuses on daytime distractions. From 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. Monday through Friday between Aug. 15 and June 15, Meta will mute most push notifications by default.

However, teens will still be able to receive direct messages. Meta will also allow account security and safety alerts during those hours. The idea is simple. A school day should come with fewer reasons to keep checking Instagram or Facebook.

Meta will also add more frequent reminders. Teens will receive a prompt after every 15 minutes of continuous screen time on Facebook or Instagram. In addition, Meta will send prompts when total daily use reaches 60 minutes and again at 90 minutes.

The settlement requires these prompts and pauses to be implemented within four months of the agreement's effective date.

Those alerts arrive before a teen reaches the two-hour limit. As a result, the hard cap becomes the final boundary rather than the first warning.

The agreement also changes parts of the viewing experience. Teens will be able to choose a non-personalized feed as their default. That feed will avoid Meta's recommendation systems when deciding what to show next.

Parents using supervision will be able to require that setting. Meta will also periodically remind teens that the option exists. Meanwhile, teens will be able to turn off autoplay. Parents will be able to require that setting too. With autoplay disabled, another piece of content will no longer begin automatically. The teen will need to tap or swipe to continue.

NEW MEXICO SEEKS MASSIVE PENALTY FROM META AFTER JURY FOUND TECH GIANT LIABLE FOR ENDANGERING CHILDREN

Meta will hide like and reaction totals by default for teen accounts. That applies to a teen's own posts as well as content posted by other people.

The company is also expanding its restrictions on appearance filters. Meta already blocks teens from using cosmetic surgery filters. Under the agreement, teens will also lose access to what Meta calls extreme makeup filters. These changes target parts of the social media experience that can keep attention focused on appearance and social feedback.

Age verification sits at the center of these protections. A teen limit only works if the platform correctly identifies the person behind the account.

Meta says it will invest in stronger technology to find accounts that may belong to children under 13. The company also plans to improve systems that identify users ages 13 to 17 who enter an adult birthday. Once Meta identifies those accounts, it can place them into experiences designed for teens.

Still, age detection remains one of the biggest tests ahead. A system that regularly mistakes teens for adults could weaken many of the protections in the agreement.

Meta also plans to expand its parental supervision tools. For example, parents will receive a notification when a teen links a secondary account. The company also plans alerts involving interactions with accounts it considers potentially suspicious.

In addition, parents will get periodic updates about their teen's usage and attempts to change protective settings. Those alerts could make it easier to catch changes without constantly checking a teen's account.

Meta began rolling out Teen Accounts in 2024. Those accounts brought automatic protections to younger Instagram users and added more control for parents. Meta later expanded its teen safety approach across more of its services.

CyberGuy previously covered Meta's expansion of Teen Accounts to Facebook and Messenger. Earlier tools leaned more heavily on reminders and configurable controls.

By comparison, the settlement creates stronger defaults. A teen who reaches the two-hour combined limit will need a parent's permission to turn it off. For a household where "five more minutes" somehow turns into another hour, that could feel very different.

Meta describes the financial package as approximately $18 billion. Participating states would receive about 70% of the allocated payment, or roughly $12.7 billion, over 10 years.

The remaining 30%, about $5.3 billion, depends on TikTok and YouTube meeting two conditions. First, both companies would need to implement a one-hour Daily Limit, Night Mode and age-assurance measures. Second, each would need to make a matching financial payment.

Half of Meta's remaining funds would be tied to YouTube's payment. The other half would depend on TikTok. Meta argues that restricting teens on one platform has limited impact if they can immediately move to another app. That helps explain why two of its biggest rivals play such a prominent role in the agreement.

The executed agreement also includes Snap in the broader industry-adoption framework. However, Meta's public explanation ties the matching financial-payment requirement specifically to TikTok and YouTube.

Meta responded to CyberGuy with additional information about the agreement, including an open letter calling on TikTok and YouTube to adopt the same framework. According to Meta, teens regularly move among many apps, so similar protections need to extend across the industry.

Meta Chief Legal Officer C.J. Mahoney made the same case in an on-camera statement provided to CyberGuy. He said, " Because teens move fluidly across dozens of apps, we need an industry-wide solution."

Mahoney also called on TikTok and YouTube to implement the framework right away. From a parent's point of view, Meta's argument is easy to understand. If Instagram closes after two hours while another social platform stays available, some teens may simply move their scrolling somewhere else.

That position also helps explain why TikTok and YouTube play such a prominent role in the settlement's financial structure.

Participation from Snap, TikTok and YouTube could trigger stricter Meta limits under the agreement's broader industry-adoption framework. The agreement requires most of its provisions to remain in place for 10 years. However, Meta's Time Limit and Night Mode commitments initially run for five years.

If industry peers join the agreement, those commitments extend to 10 years. The defaults would get tougher too.

Meta says the Daily Limit would drop to one hour per app. Night Mode would expand from midnight through 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. through 7 a.m.

As a result, participation from Meta's rivals could change both the length and strength of the restrictions.

Meta says social media platforms should not shoulder the entire age-verification process on their own. The company argues that app stores should provide developers with verified age information. According to Meta, that could help apps apply age-appropriate protections more consistently.

Meta also supports legislation that would require app stores to verify a user's age and obtain parental approval before a teen downloads an app. That debate could become increasingly important as more platforms introduce age-based restrictions.

The agreement also creates outside oversight. An independent auditor will test Meta's compliance and report to participating states. Those reviews will happen annually for five years.

Meta says the agreement will also establish an independent social media research foundation. The company says it will provide consented user data to the foundation for research into teen well-being. That outside review could help show whether the protections work once they reach millions of accounts.

A judge approved the settlement on Aug. 27. While the new requirements will roll out over the coming months, families can review their teen's social media settings today. Here are several places to start.

Meta's supervision tools give parents access to additional controls and account information. Once supervision is connected, parents can review available safety settings and manage certain protections. CyberGuy has steps showing you how to activate Instagram's parental supervision tools and link your teen's account. Before changing everything, talk with your teen about the settings you plan to use. Explain what you want to protect and why.

Open the phone's screen-time dashboard and look at the numbers together. You may discover that Instagram or Facebook takes up less time than expected. Another app could be responsible for a much larger share of the day. Then, use those numbers to set limits that reflect how the phone is actually being used. CyberGuy has a deeper guide to phone safety tools for parents, including screen-time controls.

Look at who can follow, message or tag your teen. Meta says it will continue using private defaults for teen Instagram accounts. Facebook will also keep restrictive default settings for teens. Meanwhile, the company plans to make it harder for potentially suspicious adults to find or interact with younger users. Also review followers your teen no longer recognizes.

Meta says teens will remain in age-appropriate content settings by default. The company also plans to continue restricting interactions with accounts it considers inappropriate for younger users. Parents using supervision should check those controls periodically.

Facebook and Instagram make up only part of a teen's digital day. Apple Screen Time and Google Family Link can add device-level limits. Those controls become especially useful when a teen moves from one social app to another. As a result, parents can create boundaries that extend beyond Meta's platforms.

Meta's Night Mode will add an overnight barrier inside Facebook and Instagram. Families can add another layer by charging phones outside bedrooms or keeping them in a shared space overnight. A simple routine can also reduce the nightly debate over when the phone goes away.

The two-hour cap will probably grab the most attention because it creates a clear stopping point. However, the bigger change may be how many of these protections will start turned on by default.

For teens, that could mean more interruptions during long scrolling sessions, fewer overnight opportunities to browse feeds and less pressure from notifications during school hours.

Parents will also gain more visibility when a teen tries to change certain settings. Meanwhile, Meta will face independent compliance reviews during part of the agreement period.

Age detection remains a key challenge. If a 15-year-old can easily convince the system that an account belongs to an adult, many of these protections become much easier to avoid. For that reason, the rollout will tell us far more than the announcement alone.

I have watched social media companies add parental controls for years. One recurring problem keeps coming up: Parents have to find the controls before those tools can help. This agreement puts more protections on by default. A two-hour limit that requires parental permission to disable feels very different from another screen-time reminder. The overnight block could also give families some backup when late-night scrolling becomes a constant battle. I understand Meta's argument about TikTok and YouTube too. If one app closes the door while other major platforms remain available, a teen may simply move on to the next feed. Still, the real test comes as these protections roll out over the coming months. I want to see how accurately Meta identifies teen accounts and how difficult these limits are to bypass. Parents should view these tools as backup, not autopilot. Settings can create useful boundaries, but conversations at home still have to carry much of the load.

Would you want every major social media app to automatically lock teens out after a set amount of time, or should families decide those limits themselves? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

item.title: Chicago mayor demands companies reveal whether leaders ‘reflect diversity’ for city contracts
item.description: DHS accused Brandon Johnson of punishing businesses that help ICE enforce federal immigration law after the Chicago mayor signed a new executive order.
item.content:encoded:
Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson signed an executive order on Wednesday requiring city contractors to disclose information about leadership diversity demographics, as well as report whether they have any ties to certain law enforcement agencies such as ICE, as he moves to use the city's purchasing power to impose new contracting standards.

Johnson said workplace data was necessary to identify discrimination and criticized the Trump administration's efforts to end federal reporting requirements.

"If you want to do business with this city, we want to know whether the people leading your company reflect the diversity of the communities whose tax dollars are paying your contracts," Johnson said.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) accused Johnson of punishing American companies for assisting federal immigration enforcement.

DEMOCRAT MAYOR BLASTED BY DHS FOR 'HUNTING DOWN' PROPERTY OWNERS LEASING TO ICE: 'UNHINGED'

"If Mayor Johnson wants to lecture anyone about taxpayer dollars, remember what he is: a sanctuary politician who bullies American companies with money that isn’t his. Chicago takes the federal check, but it won’t enforce the federal law," a DHS spokesperson said in a statement to Fox News Digital on Sunday.

"In case Chicago’s mayor forgot, an oath of office is a commitment to upholding the law, not encouraging criminal illegal aliens to break it," they added.

"Make no mistake, we will not be deterred. Under President Trump, ICE will keep enforcing the law in Chicago, whether City Hall likes it or not," the spokesperson said.

The Chicago mayor unveiled the order during a press conference at Arise Chicago, a nonprofit that works to protect immigrants' rights. Johnson framed the order as a response to corporate influence in Washington and said Chicago would use city spending to put its values into practice.

The order also directs Chicago's chief procurement officer to develop rules within 90 days barring vendors found to have committed public integrity, workplace discrimination or wage theft violations during the previous five years.

Contractors must disclose whether they received more than $500,000 from government or law enforcement agencies or face proceedings alleging excessive force, unlawful detention, unconstitutional policing, discrimination or other civil rights violations.

TRUMP ADMIN WANTS TO STOP ILLINOIS CITY'S REPARATIONS EFFORT FOR 'SIMPLY HANDING OUT MONEY BASED ON RACE'

Large private companies with corporate families reporting at least $1 billion in net income must provide information about leadership diversity, board composition and diversity policies when not already covered by Illinois reporting law.

Under the order, contractors must also report efforts to hire and promote formerly incarcerated people, and future awardees must update the disclosures at least annually.

Doing business with ICE alone is not listed as a disqualifying offense. The order also disqualifies firms for specified integrity, discrimination or wage theft violations while making the disclosures public.

Not With Our Money, the campaign that joined Johnson at the announcement, identified $3.19 billion in Chicago contractors held by 42 firms that also do business with ICE, according to the group's research.

DHS ISSUES SCATHING REBUKE AFTER FORMER ATLANTA MAYOR KEISHA LANCE BOTTOMS TOUTS CUTTING TIES WITH ICE

Johnson was referring to an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission proposal to rescind requirements for employers and other covered entities to file annual EEO reports containing aggregate employee race, sex and job-category data. EEOC Chair Andrea Lucas said the reports risked hindering enforcement of equal employment laws and raised constitutional concerns.

The order marks Johnson’s latest clash with federal immigration authorities.

In October, Johnson barred ICE from using city parking lots and garages for operations, a policy a federal agent said forced agents to stage in public and created operational risks. DHS said Operation Midway Blitz had resulted in more than 4,500 arrests by December.

Fox News Digital reached out to Johnson's office for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

item.title: Four foods you should never store in the freezer and where to keep them instead
item.description: Chef Dennis Littley of New Jersey reveals why cheese, cooked pasta, cured meats and wine may lose texture and flavor when stored in the freezer after thawing.
item.content:encoded:
The freezer can help food last longer, but some kitchen staples may be better off stored elsewhere.

Some foods can lose their texture, flavor or overall quality after being frozen and thawed, according to a recent list from food and cooking publication Food & Wine.

New Jersey-based Chef Dennis Littley, a culinary educator and founder of Ask Chef Dennis, told Fox News Digital that freezing can change a food's texture because the water inside turns into ice crystals.

PUMPKIN SPICE INVADES SUMMER AS AMERICANS KICKSTART FALL TRADITIONS EARLIER THAN EVER

"The biggest thing I tell home cooks is that being able to freeze something doesn't necessarily mean you should," Littley said.

Here are four foods that may be better stored somewhere other than the freezer.

While most cheeses can technically be frozen, Littley said doing so can leave them crumbly or grainy once thawed.

The change can be particularly noticeable with softer and creamier cheeses.

SCIENTISTS SAY YOU'VE BEEN THROWING AWAY PERFECTLY GOOD MEAT BECAUSE OF ONE COMMON MISTAKE

Instead, Littley recommends keeping cheese well wrapped in the refrigerator and buying only as much as you expect to use while it is still fresh.

Whether cooked pasta belongs in the freezer can depend on the dish.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"Pasta can soften as it freezes and thaws, and creamy sauces can separate," Littley said.

For pasta dishes with creamy sauces, he recommends refrigerating leftovers and eating them within a few days rather than freezing them.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Heartier baked pasta dishes, however, can hold up better in the freezer, according to Littley.

Prosciutto, salami and other cured meats can generally be frozen, but Littley said the bigger concern is what happens to their texture and flavor afterward.

That can be especially noticeable when the meat is served on a sandwich, charcuterie board or as an appetizer, where texture can be an important part of the experience.

Littley recommends keeping cured meats wrapped in the refrigerator and using them within the recommended time after opening.

Wine is one item that Littley advises keeping out of the freezer.

"No go," he said. "The liquid expands as it freezes, which can cause problems with the bottle or cork, and you're not doing the wine's flavor and aroma any favors."

Instead, opened wine should be resealed and stored in the refrigerator, including red wine.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

Red wine can then be brought back to the appropriate serving temperature before drinking, he said.

While the freezer may seem like an easy way to extend the life of many foods and drinks, Littley said proper storage can help preserve their texture, flavor and overall quality.

"Some dishes freeze beautifully, while others aren't going to come back the way you want them to," he said.
